power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Motivation shapes how people allocate cognitive control, including whether they persist with a current task or flexibly switch to another.
Although reward transitions have been shown to influence this balance, prior work has largely relied on monetary incentives.
We tested whether changes in appetitive food reward motivate voluntary task switching, and whether this effect varies with subjective reward valuation and eating-related traits.
A total of 112 undergraduate participants completed a voluntary task-switching task in which cues signaled low (1 point) or high (10 points) rewards exchangeable for candy.
Access to the candy rewards was manipulated between subjects, with a free access group and a restricted group that could see, but not access, the received candy rewards.
Trial-level choices were analyzed with generalized linear mixed models.
Participants switched tasks more often when reward value changed between trials than when it remained consistently low or high.
This reward-transition effect was larger among participants reporting greater candy liking and wanting.
It was also stronger among those more susceptible to external food cues and weaker among those reporting greater routine restraint.
Candy-access condition and progress toward the next candy did not improve model fit in the primary choice model.
These findings identify reward dynamics as a motivational influence on cognitive flexibility and extend reward-transition accounts of control allocation to primary food incentives.
Individual differences in incentive valuation and eating-related tendencies further shape how reward cues guide flexible behavior.

Cognitive control is essential for healthy, goal-directed functioning in daily life, enabling people to stay on task when distractions arise while also adapting when circumstances change (Diamond, 2013).

text.text: This capacity reflects a dynamic interplay between cognitive stability and cognitive flexibility (Musslick & Cohen, 2021).

text.text: Cognitive stability is characterized by the capability to maintain goals and task-relevant information while averting distractions, whereas cognitive flexibility encompasses the ability to engage in innovative thinking, redirect attention, and alternate between tasks in response to fluctuating environmental requirements (Banich, 2009; Egner, 2023; Fröber et al., 2018).

text.text: Although both processes are crucial, cognitive flexibility seemingly imposes significantly greater cognitive demands than maintaining stability: response times are increased for the same task when participants have to mix two or more tasks opposed to performing single task blocks, there are performance costs for switching tasks compared to repeating tasks (Monsell, 2003; Rogers & Monsell, 1995; Wylie & Allport, 2000), and when given the choice to repeat or switch tasks, participants are more likely to choose to repeat the same task (Arrington & Logan, 2004 , 2005; Mayr & Bell, 2006).

text.text: This aversion to task switching can be understood through the lens of cost-benefit analysis.
Before engaging in any task or decision, individuals naturally weigh the required effort against anticipated rewards (Croxson et al., 2009; Kool et al., 2010; Shenhav et al., 2013).

text.text: Indeed, cognitive effort is treated as an intrinsic cost that people are motivated to avoid, such that they will forgo rewards to select less demanding courses of action (Kool et al., 2010).

text.text: This principle is formalized in the Expected Value of Control (EVC) framework, which proposes that the brain-particularly the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex-computes whether to allocate cognitive control by integrating the anticipated payoff of a control-demanding action against its intrinsic effort cost (Shenhav et al., 2013).

text.text: However, motivational manipulations, particularly performance-contingent rewards, can fundamentally alter this calculation by increasing the expected value of exerting control.

High reward expectations have been shown to reduce switch costs and accelerate reaction times in task-switching paradigms by enhancing proactive control mechanisms (Chiew & Braver, 2013; Yee & Braver, 2018).

text.text: Thus, despite the inherent cognitive costs of task switching, the prospect of reward can motivate individuals to overcome their natural tendency toward cognitive stability and engage in more demanding flexible behavior.
An emerging body of work has shown that trial-to-trial dynamics of reward can differentially bias participants to stability or flexibility depending on the context.

With dynamic rewards (increases or decreases), participants are more likely to engage in flexibility with reduced switch costs and/ or a greater proportion of voluntary switches; when rewards remain stable, especially when they remain high, participants are more likely to engage in stability (Balcazar & Orr, 2025; Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016; Fröber et al., 2018; Shen & Chun, 2011).

text.text: Given that these effects of reward dynamics are contingent on participants' experienced reward value, it is necessary to examine the characteristics of the incentives used.
Reward valuation is intrinsically subjective and may be attributed to any stimulus that has innate or learned positive value (Schultz et al., 1997).

text.text: The aforementioned studies on reward transitions relied predominantly on monetary incentives, supplemented by social-competitive reward contingencies (Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016 , 2021; Shen & Chun, 2011).

text.text: While secondary rewards such as these are easy to quantify and manipulate parametrically (Elliott et al., 2003), there are important differences between abstract secondary incentives and biologically relevant primary incentives such as food (Beck et al., 2010; Rosati & Hare, 2016).

text.text: Monetary rewards-particularly checks or gift cards that constrain when and where they can be redeemed-are comparatively abstract: although adults may know their nominal value, the concrete benefit depends on how (and whether) they are ultimately spent, and redemption typically requires additional time and effort.
By contrast, food has intrinsic value.

At the same time, money rewards tend to be more broadly transferable across contexts, while food rewards are shaped by hunger and satiety levels, as well as individual preferences (Banica et al., 2023; Simon et al., 2017).

text.text: The present study investigated the extent to which appetitive food rewards modulate the trade-off between cognitive stability and cognitive flexibility.

To implement dynamic reward transitions while minimizing the potential confounding effects of satiety-related devaluation, each trial could yield 1 or 10 points, and participants received a piece of candy for every 50 accumulated points.
A progress bar displayed continuously at the bottom of the screen provided online feedback on the proximity to the next candy delivery and was reset after each dispensation.
Participants selected their preferred candy type (chocolate M&M's (Mars, Incorporated) or Original Skittles (Mars, Incorporated) fruit candies) prior to task performance.

text.text: The WREQ includes four subscales that measure how individuals control their eating: Routine Restraint (WREQ-RR), the deliberate restriction of food intake to manage weight; Compensatory Restraint (WREQ-CR), overeating followed by restraint to compensate; Susceptibility to Extenal Cues (WREQ-EX), eating in response to external cues regardless of internal hunger or satiety signals; and Emotional Eating (WREQ-EE), eating in response to negative emotions.

In addition, participants completed the Behavioral Inhibition and Behavioral Activation Systems (BIS/BAS) Scales (Carver & White, 1994), a 24-item self-report questionnaire that assesses individual differences in sensitivity to punishment and reward, with four subscales: BIS, sensitivity to punishment; BAS-Reward Responsiveness (RR), sensitivity to rewards; BAS-Fun Seeking (Fun), impulsive willingness to approach potentially rewarding events; BAS-Drive, persistent pursuit of desired goals.

text.text: Before completing the experimental task, participants completed a training phase designed to familiarize them with the reward values associated with the task cues.
The cues were blue and orange circles, which were associated with either 1 or 10 points; the color-point mapping was counterbalanced across participants.
On each training trial, one circle of each color was presented, with the circles positioned to the left and right of screen center (10 % of screen height from the center).
Each circle had a diameter equal to 8 % of screen height, and the left-right locations of the colors were randomized across trials.
The pair of circles remained onscreen for up to 3,000 ms or until the participant selected one using the up or down arrow keys.
Feedback indicating the number of points received was then displayed for 1,500 ms.
If no response was made within 3,000 ms, participants were instructed to respond more quickly.
Cue-reward validity during training matched that of the main task, although rewards in the training phase were not contingent on participants' responses.
Trials were separated by a 1,000-ms intertrial interval (ITI).
Participants completed two blocks of 10 training trials.
Each trial in the main task followed the sequence shown in Figure 1: presentation of a centrally displayed reward cue (blue or orange circle; 1,500 ms), a target display, and feedback.

text.text: The target display contained one digit (125, 132, 139, 146, 160, 167, 174, or 181) and one letter (B, D, F, H, S, U, W, or Y), presented above and below fixation, respectively, or vice versa.

text.text: Targets were positioned 10 % of screen height from the center of the display and were presented in Arial font at a size equal to 5% of screen height.
For the digit task, participants indicated whether the digit was less than or greater than 153.
For the letter task, they indicated whether the letter was closer to the beginning or end of the alphabet.

Participants responded to the upper stimulus using the left-hand keys ("D" and "F") and to the lower stimulus using the right-hand keys ("J" and "K"); the mapping of target position to response hand was counterbalanced across participants.
The target display remained onscreen until a response was made or 3,000 ms had elapsed, after which feedback was displayed for 1,500 ms.
During both training and the reward portion of the experiment, a reward progress bar was continuously displayed at the bottom of the screen.
The bar filled as participants earned points and reset after they accumulated 50 points, at which point a candy reward was dispensed.
Before beginning the task, participants selected either chocolate M &M's (Mars, Incorporated) or Original Skittles (Mars, Incorporated) as their reward.

text.text: PsychoPy controlled the dispenser through a USB relay (ADU200; OnTrak Control Systems Inc., Canada).
When participants accumulated 50 points, a TTL pulse triggered delivery of a single piece of candy simultaneously with the feedback display.

Although the dispenser's infrared sensor was designed to prevent the release of multiple candies, it occasionally dispensed more than one piece; these occurrences were not monitored or recorded consistently.
Candy was dispensed into a metal bowl lined with a paper coffee filter for hygiene.
Although participants were instructed to maintain fixation on the screen, the audible sound of the candy entering the bowl indicated that a reward had been delivered.
As shown in Figure 2, the study included two candy-access conditions.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>, the study included two candy-access conditions.

text.text: In the Free Access condition, participants could view and access the candies they earned throughout the session, although they were instructed to wait until the next break before consuming them.
In the Restricted Access condition, the dispenser was placed inside a previously concealed clear acrylic box with a locking lid after the training phase.
Participants could view the earned candies but were informed that they would not be able to access them until the end of the experimental session.
Following the training phase, but before starting the primary task, participants individually practiced the two tasks.
They were given eight trials to reach 80% accuracy; if they did not meet criterion, the experimenter reviewed the instructions, confirmed understanding, and the practice was repeated.
After successful practice of each task, participants practiced switching between the two tasks ("Try to perform a mix of both tasks and not just focusing on a single task").

Participants completed 16 trials and repeated this practice if they did not achieve at least 80% accuracy and/or if their switch rate fell outside 15%-85%; before each repeat, the experimenter again verified that the participant understood the task and emphasized balancing the two tasks.

If a participant failed to meet criteria after three attempts in any practice phase, the session was terminated because persistent noncompliance was taken to indicate that the participant was not making a good-faith effort to perform the task.
In order to set reaction time thresholds for fast responses in reward trials, participants first completed 64 trials without performance contingencies and without rewards.
Although the cues were presented, participants were instructed to ignore them.
No progress bar was shown, and the feedback contained information only about the accuracy of the response.
From this block, an initial threshold of the 40th percentile was set for the rewarded blocks.
Separate reaction time thresholds were calculated for each task and task transition (repeat or switching).
The thresholds were updated after each block, based on all cumulative correct trials.
On error trials, the feedback said "Error," and on trials in which a response was not made within 3000 ms, it said "Please respond!!".
Participants completed 8 blocks of 32 trials during the reward phase.

In line with studies by Fröber, Dreissbach, and colleagues (Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016; Fröber et al., 2018), for 1-point trials, there was no speed requirement to receive the point, only an accuracy requirement.

text.text: For 10-point trials, points were given only if the response was correct and faster than the speed threshold.
If the response was correct, but not fast enough, the participant received 0 points and feedback that said "Respond Faster!".
If participants made an error or did not respond within 3000 ms, they lost 5 points, and the progress bar receded.
Before the training phase, the dispenser was partially filled with the candy that the participants chose.
They were asked to indicate on a continuous slider how much they liked the candy they chose.
The slider contained 5 tick marks, and the beginning and end were anchored by "Not At All" and "A Lot", respectively.
Then they were asked to indicate how much they wanted to eat the candy, using the same slider.
After each block, they were asked how much they wanted additional candy, and, in the Free access version, they were also asked how much they liked the candy they just received.
All analyses were carried out in R (R Core Team, 2026).
Voluntary task choice, i.e. the decision to repeat or switch tasks, as well as reaction times, were analyzed using (generalized) linear mixed models using trial-level data.
Accuracy was not analyzed because the performance was near ceiling (Median = 0.972, IQR = 0.031).

To examine task switch proportions, we used a generalized linear mixed model with task transition (repeat: 0, switch: 1) as a binary dependent measure and a binomial distribution family with a logit link function.
We evaluated multiple models to determine which provided the best fit.

Each model examined the effect of reward transition, i.e., the interaction between the previous trial's reward outcome (hereafter referred to as 'previous trial reward') and the current trial's reward prospect (hereafter referred to as 'current trial reward').

We also evaluated additive and interactive terms for the candy access version (free vs. restricted) and a continuous indicator of how many points remained until the next candy reward (i.e., reward progress).
Reward progress was included to assess whether participant's behavior was affected by proximity to the goal, i.e. candy receipt.
Model fits were compared using the Akaike Information Criteria corrected for small sample bias and likelihood ratio tests to identify significant differences.

For each model, we identified the most parsimonious random-effects structure following recommendations by Bates et al. (Bates et al., 2018) beginning with a maximal structure and simplifying it when convergence problems occurred.

text.text: We included the block number as a random factor to account for the variability throughout the duration of the experiment, such as fatigue and satiety for the candy rewards.
To examine whether the reward transition effect was moderated by how much the participant 1) liked the candy rewards and 2) wanted more candy, we ran separate analyses with these ratings.
Because participants were unable to eat candy during the restricted access version, we restricted the analysis of the liking ratings to the free access version.
For the analysis of the wanting ratings, we evaluated whether treating candy access version as an additive and interactive term best fit the data.

To examine individual differences, we performed separate analyses that included responses to self-report questionnaires (demographics, substance use, BIS-BAS, and the Weight-Related Eating Questionnaire).
We only included those who self-reported male and female gender, excluding those who identified as non-binary or transgender due to low response numbers.
Gender was also coded as a sum contrast.
Because the BIS-BAS and the Weight-Related Eating Questionnaire subscales were correlated, we performed a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce complexity and collinearity (see details below).
To examine individual differences in reward-guided cognitive flexibility, separate models were fit for each of the PCA component scores.
In order to interpret models where PCA scores had a significant contribution, we compared models with a given PCA score included as an additive factor or an interactive factor.

text.text: To facilitate the interpretation of individual differences and reduce collinearity between the eight BIS-BAS and WREQ subscale scores, PCA-derived component scores were examined.
Based on the scree plot and cumulative variance explained (approximately 80%), four components were retained (see Supplemental Table A1 for factor loadings).

text.text: The first component (PC1) showed moderate positive loadings on nearly all subscales except BIS, suggesting a general tendency toward increased motivational responsiveness.

The second component (PC2) was characterized by moderate negative loadings on the BAS subscales, particularly Reward Responsiveness, and moderate positive loadings on the WREQ subscales, particularly Routine Restraint and Emotional Eating, reflecting greater responsiveness to eating-related and affective influences alongside lower responsiveness to rewarding outcomes.
The third component (PC3) was defined by a strong positive loading on BIS, reflecting a greater sensitivity to potential negative outcomes.

The fourth component (PC4) exhibited moderately strong positive loadings on Routine Restraint (WREQ-RR) and moderately strong negative loadings on Susceptibility to External Cues (WREQ-EX), indicating a tendency to restrict food intake rather than respond to external food cues in the absence of internal hunger or satiety signals.
Subsequently, these component scores were used to examine whether individual differences in motivational and eating-related tendencies moderated the probability of the switch (see below).
The best fitting model for switch probability did not contain interactive terms for candy access version or reward progress.

text.text: There was a significant two-way interaction of previous reward outcome and current reward prospect.
This indicates that the effect of current reward prospect on the odds of switching depended on the previous reward outcome.
Specifically, the odds ratio for current high versus low reward was 44% lower following a high previous reward than following a low previous reward.

As shown in Figure 3, and supported by a planned contrast of changing reward versus consistent reward, participants switched tasks 20.1% more often when the reward increased or decreased than when the reward was consistently low or high.

text.text: We were also interested in how individual differences captured by the BIS-BAS and WREQ subscales moderated the effect of reward transition.
In separate analyses, we included factor loadings for PC1, PC2, PC3, and PC4 in the model of the main analysis described above.
Model fit comparisons for each of these analyses are reported in Supplementary Table A8.

text.text: The PC4 component was characterized by a positive loading of routine restraint in eating (WREQ-RR) and a negative loading of cue-driven eating (WREQ-EX).
As shown in Figure 5, the reward transition effect was greatest at low levels of PC4 and smallest at high levels of PC4.

text.text: To interpret this finding in terms of the original variables, we derived predicted probabilities from the fitted model by substituting implied PC4 scores.

For each variable (WREQ-RR, WREQ-EX), we computed the PC4 score that would result from that variable being at -1SD (Low) , 0SD (Average), or +1SD (High) while holding the other two variables at their mean (0 after scaling).

These implied PC4 scores were entered into the original model to generate predicted switch probabilities across all combinations of previous reward and current reward, marginalized over candy access version.

This approach allows the contribution of each variable to the three-way interaction to be examined without fitting additional models, while respecting the correlational structure that motivated the PCA.

The predicted switch probabilities for the three subscales are shown in Supplemental Figures B2 and B3, and the comparisons of the reward transition effect within and between the levels of each subscale are reported in Supplemental Table 6.

The pattern was in the opposing direction for WREQ-EX, with a larger reward transition effect at high than at average or low levels, as well as a larger effect at the average level than at the low level.

As previous studies have found reduced switch costs with changing reward compared to consistent reward, we first sought to test if this pattern was replicated here.
To simplify the visualization of switch cost for each combination of previous and current reward, we combined previous and current reward to a single factor, reward transition.

As shown in Figure 6, and confirmed by post-hoc testing, the switch cost was lower with changing reward (Increase and Decrease) compared to consistent reward (Remain Low and Remain High; ∆RT = 63.4 ms, 95% CI = [43.1, 83.8]).

text.text: Finally, none of the models with interactive factors of the Principal Components had a better fit than the model without these factors.

This study tested whether dynamic changes in point amounts-where one candy was earned for every 50 points-influence the trade-off between cognitive stability and flexibility, as previously shown with monetary incentives.

Despite important differences between food and money, point transitions robustly altered control allocation: participants voluntarily switched tasks more often when point values changed than when they remained constant.
This reward transition effect scaled with individual differences in reward sensitivity, including liking and wanting ratings and eating-related traits.
Together, these results show that sensitivity to changing reward value plays an important role in reward-guided cognitive flexibility.

Previous work indicates that transitions in reward availability act as a meta-control signal regulating the stability-flexibility trade-off, with increased voluntary switching and reduced switch costs when reward changes relative to a consistent context.
These effects are attenuated or absent under probabilistic reward schedules with cue-outcome validity below 80% (Balcazar & Orr, 2025; Orr et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These effects are attenuated or absent under probabilistic reward schedules with cue-outcome validity below 80% <ref type="bibr">(Balcazar & Orr, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Orr et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present data extend this signal to a primary reward.

A three-way interaction among task alternation, previous reward, and current reward showed that switch costs were reduced when reward levels changed relative to when they stayed the same, supporting our first hypothesis.

Importantly, choice behavior mirrored this pattern: participants switched more when rewards changed, consistent with prior studies showing that changing reward structure encourages flexibility and exploration (Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016; Shen & Chun, 2011).
text.formatted: Importantly, choice behavior mirrored this pattern: participants switched more when rewards changed, consistent with prior studies showing that changing reward structure encourages flexibility and exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Shen & Chun, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Participants also switched less for repeated high rewards than for repeated low rewards, and more when rewards decreased than when they increased.
Two interpretations could help explain this pattern.
First, reward transitions may signal environmental change, shifting control toward a more exploratory mode, as in adaptive gain theory (Aston-Jones & Cohen, 2005).
text.formatted: First, reward transitions may signal environmental change, shifting control toward a more exploratory mode, as in adaptive gain theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Aston-Jones & Cohen, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Second, repeated high rewards may foster satisfaction that reduces the motivation to seek alternatives, whereas a decrease in reward signals that the current strategy is suboptimal.
A reduction in an expected reward can also produce frustrative non-reward, which may serve as a catalyst for behavioral adjustment (Abler et al., 2005; Amsel, 1992).
text.formatted: A reduction in an expected reward can also produce frustrative non-reward, which may serve as a catalyst for behavioral adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abler et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amsel, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: This account fits evidence that bottom-up influences on task switching are typically limited to task-relevant stimuli (Jurczyk et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This account fits evidence that bottom-up influences on task switching are typically limited to task-relevant stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Jurczyk et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Reaction times also decreased as participants neared the candy reward, particularly in the high-reward condition.

Because the progress bar was continuously visible, this pattern is more consistent with the salience hypothesis of goal monitoring-in which monitoring and effort increase as a goal becomes imminent-than with the uncertainty hypothesis-in which progress is checked regularly to reduce uncertainty (Devine et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Because the progress bar was continuously visible, this pattern is more consistent with the salience hypothesis of goal monitoring-in which monitoring and effort increase as a goal becomes imminent-than with the uncertainty hypothesis-in which progress is checked regularly to reduce uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Devine et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It is also consistent with studies that show that participants increased effort near goal completion when progress was visible (Sayalı et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It is also consistent with studies that show that participants increased effort near goal completion when progress was visible <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Sayalı et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, we did not measure how often participants looked at the progress bar, so this interpretation remains tentative.

The reward-transition effect on reaction-time switch costs was not specific to restricted candy access: switch costs were lower for changing than for consistent reward transitions, but this effect did not differ significantly by access version.
Adding access version also did not improve fit in the primary choice model.
However, access effects were not uniformly absent: in the wanting rating analysis, the reward-transition effect varied jointly with wanting and access version.
Delay can reduce the subjective value of a reward, but clear progress toward a goal can sustain motivation despite the delay (Howe et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Delay can reduce the subjective value of a reward, but clear progress toward a goal can sustain motivation despite the delay <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Howe et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This may help to explain why there were not more robust effects of the candy access version.
The benefits of reward transitions were tied to the reward environment.
Under restricted access, but not free access, we replicated monetary findings of reduced switch costs for changing versus consistent rewards (Fröber & Dreisbach, 2016; Shen & Chun, 2011).

text.text: Restricted candy access and typical monetary paradigms share a delay in reward receipt: participants received the candy only after the experiment, like a delayed gift card.
However, delay alone cannot explain our results, because a previous study with delayed monetary rewards found no differences in switch costs across reward transitions (Orr et al., 2025).

text.text: D What distinguishes the present paradigm is that a primary reward was visible but withheld.

Palatable food cues without consumption induce anticipatory autonomic and endocrine responses as well as craving (Power & Schulkin, 2008; Smeets et al., 2012), similar to the cue reactivity seen in addiction research (Betts et al., 2021; Carter & Tiffany, 1999).
text.formatted: Palatable food cues without consumption induce anticipatory autonomic and endocrine responses as well as craving <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Power & Schulkin, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Smeets et al., 2012)</ref>, similar to the cue reactivity seen in addiction research <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Betts et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Carter & Tiffany, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Restricting access to the candy therefore likely created a motivationally engaging state, with a persistent conflict between urges and the no-eating rule that secondary rewards do not readily produce.
Our second hypothesis was also supported: individual differences in reward responsiveness and eating styles significantly modulated the relationship between reward transitions and cognitive control.
First, participants who reported higher levels of liking and wanting the candy showed a greater effect of reward transitions on task switching.
This finding highlights the role of individual differences in motivational salience and aligns with neurobiological models of reward processing.
Liking generally refers to the pleasurable, hedonic enjoyment experienced when consuming a reward.
Wanting, in contrast, describes the motivational drive to seek out and obtain that reward and is more closely tied to dopaminergic signaling (Morales & Berridge, 2020; Pool et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Wanting, in contrast, describes the motivational drive to seek out and obtain that reward and is more closely tied to dopaminergic signaling <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Morales & Berridge, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Pool et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the influence of wanting on behavior was slightly stronger than that of liking, echoing findings from addiction research.

It is possible to strongly desire a reward without necessarily deriving pleasure from its consumption, a phenomenon well-documented in substance use research (Grigutsch et al., 2019; Koranyi et al., 2017; Robinson & Berridge, 2025).
text.formatted: It is possible to strongly desire a reward without necessarily deriving pleasure from its consumption, a phenomenon well-documented in substance use research <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Grigutsch et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Koranyi et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Robinson & Berridge, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, participants who reported high levels of wanting may have been driven more by the motivational pull of the candy reward than by the actual anticipated enjoyment of consuming it, thereby showing greater sensitivity to reward transitions and a stronger tendency to switch tasks.
We also examined whether individual differences measured by the BIS/BAS personality scales and the Weight-Related Eating Questionnaire (WREQ) were associated with the reward-transition effect.
The moderating component identified in these analyses was characterized most strongly by self-reported routine restraint and susceptibility to external food cues.
Participants reporting greater routine restraint showed a smaller reward-transition effect, whereas those reporting greater cue-driven eating showed a larger effect.

Because the WREQ assesses reported eating behaviors, these findings are best CANDY REWARDS & FLEXIBILITY 20 interpreted as associations between eating-related tendencies and task choice, rather than as evidence that personality traits caused differences in switching.
text.formatted: Because the WREQ assesses reported eating behaviors, these findings are best CANDY REWARDS & FLEXIBILITY 20 interpreted as associations between eating-related tendencies and task choice, rather than as evidence that personality traits caused differences in switching.

text.text: For people highly sensitive to external food cues, salient restricted food cues can heighten craving and arousal (Carter & Tiffany, 1999).
text.formatted: For people highly sensitive to external food cues, salient restricted food cues can heighten craving and arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Carter & Tiffany, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Resisting the visible reward then demands strong top-down prefrontal control (Kober et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Resisting the visible reward then demands strong top-down prefrontal control <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kober et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Sustained prefrontal recruitment to regulate cue-reactivity leaves fewer resources for task switching, selectively impairing cognitive flexibility and increasing rigidity during reward transitions.

By contrast, individuals low on affect-driven scales may use reduced reward value or disappointment as a signal to adapt: rather than draining control, low reward or errors appear to increase sensitivity to reward changes and promote task switching to seek better options, likely due to more balanced reward-system activation.

First, this was a behavioral study and was not designed to test neural or physiological mechanisms; eye tracking of progress-bar monitoring, EEG/fMRI, and skin conductance could test the mechanisms proposed here.
Second, reward variety was limited to two candies (M&Ms and Skittles) because of the dispenser's physical constraints, and some participants may not have found these rewarding.
text.formatted: Second, reward variety was limited to two candies (M&Ms and Skittles) because of the dispenser's physical constraints, and some participants may not have found these rewarding.

text.text: Third, we did not assess hunger at the start of the session; time of day, recent food intake, and eating schedules may have influenced the initial desirability of the candy.

Future studies could examine whether people with difficulty controlling eating, such as those with strong cravings or a history of disordered eating, or with a history of addiction, show different reward-mediated flexibility, given their altered reward sensitivity and cognitive control.

It would also be useful to determine whether effects arise from sugar or from other features of candy (flavor, texture, emotional associations) by comparing candy with pure sugar and by developing dispensers for savory, non-sugary foods.
Collectively, these findings suggest that reward dynamics involving primary food incentives can shape voluntary task switching, with effects that vary across individuals.

The present analyses do not show that restricted access improves behavioral adaptation relative to free access, nor do they establish that food rewards affect cognitive control differently from monetary incentives.
Potential neurobiological and physiological mechanisms remain hypotheses for future research.

For individuals characterized by affect-driven eating behaviors, the prefrontal demands of regulating appetitive cravings in highly rewarding, restricted-access environments may deplete executive resources, leading to cognitive rigidity.
In contrast, for others, the disappointment of delayed or suboptimal rewards acts as a motivating cue for exploration and adaptation.

This work contributes to a deeper, more integrated understanding of how cognitive effort is shaped by motivational contexts, offering valuable implications for understanding both adaptive goal pursuit and maladaptive self-regulation failures.
